The samples suggest, but do not prove, that sixth graders like the hours more.
Seventh graders like the hours more, since 24 is a greater number than 12.
The samples show nothing at all, since the two samples are different sizes.
questions.answer: The samples suggest, but do not prove, that sixth graders like the hours more.
questions.solution: Sixth graders: $\frac{12}{15} = 80\%$. Seventh graders: $\frac{24}{40} = 60\%$. The sixth graders in the samples like the hours more. Samples can only suggest what is true for everyone. Different sample sizes are fine when we compare fractions or percents.

solve.answer: The samples suggest, but do not prove, that sixth graders like the hours more.
solve.work: 12/15 = 80% vs 24/40 = 60%. Compare rates, not counts; the samples suggest sixth graders like the hours more but do not prove it.

questions.skill: Word a survey question fairly
questions.stem: A survey asks, "Our wonderful new park has great playground equipment. How much do you enjoy the park?" Why is this question a problem?
choices: The wording pushes people toward a positive answer.
The question is about a park instead of about a school.
The question is too short to give useful results.
The question does not ask about the people who use the park.
questions.answer: The wording pushes people toward a positive answer.
questions.solution: Calling the park "wonderful" with "great" equipment suggests the answer the writer wants. A fair question would ask about the park without praising it.

solve.answer: The wording pushes people toward a positive answer.
solve.work: 'Wonderful' and 'great' lead respondents toward a positive answer.

questions.skill: Word a survey question fairly
questions.stem: Three survey questions are listed. (1) Which do you prefer, cats or dogs? (2) Don't you agree that dogs are better than cats? (3) Dogs are wonderful, so which pet do you like better? How many of these three questions are worded fairly?
questions.solution: Question (1) gives both choices without a hint. Question (2) leads people to agree, and question (3) praises dogs first. So only 1 question is worded fairly.

questions.skill: Combine several random samples
questions.stem: A jar holds 500 marbles, some red and the rest blue. Four different random samples of 20 marbles each have 4, 6, 5 and 5 red marbles. Use all four samples together to estimate how many red marbles are in the jar.
questions.solution: Together the samples hold $4 \times 20 = 80$ marbles, and $4 + 6 + 5 + 5 = 20$ of them are red. That is $\frac{20}{80} = \frac{1}{4}$. A quarter of 500 marbles is $500 \div 4 = 125$.

solve.work: Red in samples: 4 + 6 + 5 + 5 = 20 of 80 = 1/4. Estimate 1/4 x 500 = 125.

questions.skill: Sample size and reliability
questions.stem: Two students each want to estimate the fraction of 900 students who like the school mascot. Ana asks 15 students chosen at random. Ben asks 150 students chosen at random. Whose estimate is likely to be closer to the true fraction, and why?
choices: Ana's, because a smaller sample has less bias
Neither, because random samples are never close to the truth
Ben's, because a larger random sample varies less
They are equally likely to be close, because both samples are random
questions.answer: Ben's, because a larger random sample varies less
questions.solution: Both samples are random, so neither is biased. But a small sample can easily land far from the true fraction by chance, while a larger random sample tends to stay close to it. Ben's sample of 150 is more likely to give a good estimate.

solve.answer: Ben's, because a larger random sample varies less
solve.work: Larger random samples have less sampling variability, so Ben's estimate is likely closer.

questions.skill: Draw a random sample with random numbers
questions.stem: Mr. Lee numbers his 30 students from 01 to 30. He reads two-digit numbers in order from a list of random numbers. He keeps each number that is from 01 to 30 and is not already chosen, and he stops when 4 students are chosen. The list is 31, 17, 45, 08, 17, 30, 09, 25. What is the number of the fourth student chosen?
questions.solution: Go through the list in order. 31 is too big, so skip it. 17 is kept (first). 45 is too big. 08 is kept (second). 17 has already been chosen, so skip it. 30 is kept (third). 09 is kept (fourth). The fourth student is number 09, which is 9.

solve.issues: Student may type 09; the key should accept 9 and 09 as the same number.
solve.work: 31 skip; 17 first; 45 skip; 08 second; 17 repeat skip; 30 third; 09 fourth. Stop.

questions.skill: Recognize a statistical question
questions.stem: Which question can be answered by collecting data that will vary from student to student?
choices: Which sport did Lena play with her cousins at the park last Saturday?
How many players are allowed on the field for one soccer team at a time?
What is the name of the ball that is used in a basketball game?
Which sport do seventh graders at our school like best: soccer or golf?
questions.answer: Which sport do seventh graders at our school like best: soccer or golf?
questions.solution: Different seventh graders may name different sports, so we must ask many students and the answers vary. A statistical question can have a category as its answer. The other questions have one answer each.

solve.answer: Which sport do seventh graders at our school like best: soccer or golf?
solve.work: Seventh graders' favorite of soccer/golf varies student to student. The others have a single answer (ball name, Lena's one sport, a fixed rule).

questions.skill: Write or choose a question that compares two groups
questions.stem: Mr. Reed wants to know whether students who eat breakfast do better on spelling quizzes than students who do not. Which data should he collect from each student?
choices: Only the score that the student earned on the spelling quiz
Only whether or not the student eats breakfast in the morning
The student's favorite breakfast food and favorite school subject
Whether the student eats breakfast, and the student's quiz score
questions.answer: Whether the student eats breakfast, and the student's quiz score
questions.solution: He needs to sort the students into two groups (breakfast or no breakfast) and also to have a score for each student. Scores alone cannot be split into groups, and groups alone give nothing to compare.

solve.answer: Whether the student eats breakfast, and the student's quiz score
solve.work: To compare groups he needs the group (breakfast or not) and the outcome (quiz score) for each student.

questions.skill: Write or choose a question that compares two groups
questions.stem: Which statistical question can be answered by collecting measurements from two groups?
choices: Is the typical 100-meter time shorter for seventh graders than sixth graders?
Are the seventh graders at our school more athletic than the sixth graders are?
Who is the fastest seventh grader at our school this school year?
Do the sixth graders at our school enjoy running in gym class?
questions.answer: Is the typical 100-meter time shorter for seventh graders than sixth graders?
questions.solution: The first question names a measurement (time to run 100 meters), two groups and a comparison of typical values. "More athletic" is not measured, the fastest student is one person, and the last question is about only one group.

solve.answer: Is the typical 100-meter time shorter for seventh graders than sixth graders?
solve.work: 100-meter times are measurements from two groups. 'Fastest' has one answer; 'more athletic' is not a measurement; enjoyment is one group.

questions.skill: Population and sample
questions.stem: A city has 12,000 residents. A survey is sent to a random sample of 150 residents. What percent of the residents are in the sample?
questions.solution: The sample is $\frac{150}{12000}$ of the population. $150 \div 12000 = 0.0125$, which is $1.25$ percent.

questions.skill: Spot and explain bias in a sample
questions.stem: A researcher wants to estimate how many hours per week students at a school exercise. She surveys students at the school gym on a Saturday morning. Which change would most reduce bias?
choices: Choose students at random from a list of all the students
Survey many more students who are at the gym on Saturdays
Survey the students at the gym on both Saturday and Sunday
Survey only the students who are on a school sports team
questions.answer: Choose students at random from a list of all the students
questions.solution: The bias comes from where the students are found: people at the gym probably exercise more than other students. A random choice from the list of all students gives each student the same chance. Surveying more people from the gym keeps the same bias.

solve.answer: Choose students at random from a list of all the students
solve.work: Gym-goers exercise more. Random selection from the full list removes the selection bias; more gym-goers or sports-team students keep it.

questions.skill: Spot and explain bias in a sample
questions.stem: Two surveys estimate how many hours per week the students at a middle school spend on sports. Survey A asks 100 students picked at random from a list of all students. Survey B asks 400 students who stay for the after-school sports clubs. Which statement is true?
choices: Survey B is probably better, because it asks more students than Survey A.
Survey A is probably better, because it is random even though it is smaller.
The two surveys are equally good, because they ask about the same topic.
Survey A is probably biased, because it asks fewer students than Survey B.
questions.answer: Survey A is probably better, because it is random even though it is smaller.
questions.solution: Students in the sports clubs probably spend more time on sports than other students, so Survey B is biased, however many students it includes. Survey A gives every student the same chance of being chosen. A bigger sample does not fix bias.

solve.answer: Survey A is probably better, because it is random even though it is smaller.
solve.work: B surveys only sports-club students: biased toward more sports regardless of size. A is random, so better.

questions.skill: Spot and explain bias in a sample
questions.stem: A researcher chooses 50 students at random for a survey, but 30 of them do not return it. She uses only the 20 surveys that were returned. What problem might this cause?
choices: There is no problem, because the first 50 students were chosen at random.
The survey now has too many questions for the 20 students who answered.
The results are correct as long as all 20 students are in the same grade.
The 20 who returned it may not be like the 30 who did not, so it may be biased.
questions.answer: The 20 who returned it may not be like the 30 who did not, so it may be biased.
questions.solution: Students who answer a survey can differ from students who do not. Using only the returned surveys can leave out a kind of student, even though the first 50 were random, so the results may be biased.

solve.answer: The 20 who returned it may not be like the 30 who did not, so it may be biased.
solve.work: Nonresponse bias: those who returned it may differ from those who did not.

questions.skill: Choose a random sampling method
questions.stem: A middle school has 200 students in grade 6, 150 in grade 7 and 150 in grade 8. The student council wants a random sample of 50 students in which each grade is represented in proportion to its size. Which plan does this?
choices: Choose 16 students at random from grade 6, 17 from grade 7 and 17 from grade 8
Choose 20 students at random from grade 6, 15 from grade 7 and 15 from grade 8
Choose all 50 students at random from the students who are in grade 7
Choose the first 50 students that you see in the lunch line
questions.answer: Choose 20 students at random from grade 6, 15 from grade 7 and 15 from grade 8
questions.solution: Grade 6 has $\frac{200}{500} = 40\%$ of the students, so it should give 40% of 50 = 20 students. Grades 7 and 8 each have 30%, which is 15 students. The other plans are not in proportion or are not random.

solve.answer: Choose 20 students at random from grade 6, 15 from grade 7 and 15 from grade 8

questions.skill: Choose a random sampling method
questions.stem: A school has 400 students in grade 6, 300 in grade 7 and 300 in grade 8. A random sample of 60 students is to be chosen so that each grade is represented in proportion to its size. How many students should be chosen from grade 7?
questions.solution: Grade 7 has 300 of the 1,000 students, which is $\frac{300}{1000} = 30\%$. So 30% of 60 is $0.3 \times 60 = 18$ students.

questions.skill: Why a random sample represents a population, and how samples vary
questions.stem: Dev takes many random samples of 10 candies from a huge bowl, and Mia takes many random samples of 100 candies from the same bowl. Each records the fraction of sour candies. Whose fractions will most likely be closer to each other?
choices: Mia's, because larger random samples vary less from sample to sample.
Dev's, because smaller random samples vary less from sample to sample.
They are equally close, because all of the samples are random.
Neither, because the fractions will be exactly the same each time.
questions.answer: Mia's, because larger random samples vary less from sample to sample.
questions.solution: A small random sample can easily have a very different share of sour candies by chance. A larger random sample tends to stay closer to the true share, so Mia's fractions are closer together.

solve.answer: Mia's, because larger random samples vary less from sample to sample.
solve.work: Larger random samples have less sampling variability, so Mia's fractions cluster more closely.

questions.skill: Why a random sample represents a population, and how samples vary
questions.stem: Mia wants to estimate the fraction of 2,000 students who walk to school. She takes a random sample of 80. A friend says that if she doubles the sample to 160, the estimate will be exactly right. Is the friend correct?
choices: Yes. A sample of 160 is bigger than 80, so the estimate will be exact.
No. A larger random sample always gives a worse estimate than a small one.
No. A larger random sample is usually better, but it is still not exact.
Yes. The number 160 is a multiple of 80, so it works out exactly.
questions.answer: No. A larger random sample is usually better, but it is still not exact.
questions.solution: A larger random sample tends to be closer to the true fraction, but it is still only a sample. Only asking all 2,000 students would give the exact fraction.

solve.answer: No. A larger random sample is usually better, but it is still not exact.
solve.work: A larger sample tends to be closer but is still an estimate, never guaranteed exact.

questions.skill: Why a random sample represents a population, and how samples vary
questions.stem: Which statement about random samples is correct?
choices: A random sample always has exactly the same percents as the population does.
A sample can, by chance, differ from the population in the share of a group.
A random sample can never include members from a large group in the population.
A random sample is always biased, even when chance picks the members.
questions.answer: A sample can, by chance, differ from the population in the share of a group.
questions.solution: Because chance picks the members, a sample can have somewhat more or fewer members of a group than the population has. That is why estimates from samples are approximate.

solve.answer: A sample can, by chance, differ from the population in the share of a group.
solve.work: By chance a random sample can differ from the population in a group's share; the other statements are false.

questions.skill: Estimate a population count or percent from a random sample
questions.stem: In a random sample of 120 students from a district, 45 say they prefer online homework and the rest prefer paper homework. The district has 8,400 students. About how many more students in the district prefer paper homework than prefer online homework?
questions.solution: Online: $\frac{45}{120} \times 8400 = 3150$ students. Paper: $\frac{75}{120} \times 8400 = 5250$ students. The difference is $5250 - 3150 = 2100$.

questions.skill: Estimate a population count or percent from a random sample
questions.stem: A biologist catches 50 fish from a pond, tags them and puts them back. Later she catches a random sample of 40 fish and finds that 5 of them are tagged. About how many fish are in the pond?
questions.solution: $\frac{5}{40}$ of the sample are tagged, so about $\frac{1}{8}$ of all the fish in the pond are tagged. The 50 tagged fish are $\frac{1}{8}$ of the pond, so the pond has about $50 \times 8 = 400$ fish.

solve.work: Tagged share in sample 5/40 = 1/8 estimates 50/N. N = 50 x 8 = 400.

questions.skill: Estimate a population count or percent from a random sample
questions.stem: A manager checks a random sample of 45 of the 1,800 packages in a warehouse and finds 3 that are damaged. Each damaged package costs 12 dollars to replace. About how many dollars would it cost to replace all the damaged packages in the warehouse?
questions.solution: $\frac{3}{45} = \frac{1}{15}$ of the packages are damaged. $1800 \div 15 = 120$ damaged packages. At 12 dollars each, that is $120 \times 12 = 1440$ dollars.

questions.skill: Estimate a population mean or median from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 25 seventh graders from a school of 400 seventh graders has a mean of 40 minutes of homework per night. Estimate the total number of minutes of homework done by all 400 seventh graders in one night.
questions.solution: Estimate that the mean for the whole school is also 40 minutes. For 400 students, the total is about $40 \times 400 = 16{,}000$ minutes.

solve.work: Estimated mean 40 min per student x 400 students = 16000 minutes.

questions.skill: Simulate a sample with random numbers or a device
questions.stem: Eli numbers the 24 students in his class from 01 to 24. To choose a random sample of 3 students, he reads random two-digit numbers: 47, 12, 88, 05, 12, 31, 19, 22. He skips any number that is not from 01 to 24 and any number he has already chosen. What is the sum of the numbers of the three students chosen?
questions.solution: 47 is too big, so skip it. 12 is chosen. 88 is too big. 05 is chosen. 12 is a repeat, so skip it. 31 is too big. 19 is chosen, which makes three students. The sum is $12 + 5 + 19 = 36$.

solve.work: 47 skip; 12 chosen; 88 skip; 05 chosen; 12 repeat skip; 31 skip; 19 chosen (3 found). Sum 12 + 5 + 19 = 36.

questions.skill: Simulate a sample with random numbers or a device
questions.stem: A basketball player makes 40% of her shots. In a simulation, the digits 0 through 3 mean "make" and the digits 4 through 9 mean "miss". One trial is 5 simulated shots. Five trials gave these digits. Trial 1: 6, 2, 9, 8, 7. Trial 2: 1, 7, 3, 4, 5. Trial 3: 0, 3, 8, 9, 6. Trial 4: 5, 9, 7, 4, 8. Trial 5: 2, 0, 1, 3, 9. In how many of the 5 trials did the player make at least 2 shots?
questions.solution: Count the makes (digits 0 to 3) in each trial: Trial 1 has 1 (the 2). Trial 2 has 2 (1 and 3). Trial 3 has 2 (0 and 3). Trial 4 has 0. Trial 5 has 4 (2, 0, 1, 3). Trials 2, 3 and 5 have at least 2 makes, so the answer is 3.

questions.skill: Simulate a sample with random numbers or a device
questions.stem: Mia guesses on all 10 questions of a true-or-false quiz. She wants to estimate the chance of getting at least 8 right by guessing. She will use a fair coin, with heads meaning a right answer. Which plan is best?
choices: Flip the coin 10 times one time and check whether there are at least 8 heads in all
Flip the coin until 8 heads in a row appear, then count the number of flips
Flip the coin 8 times for one quiz and count how many heads there are
Flip 10 times for one quiz, repeat many times, and count quizzes with at least 8 heads
questions.answer: Flip 10 times for one quiz, repeat many times, and count quizzes with at least 8 heads
questions.solution: One simulated quiz is 10 flips. A single quiz is not enough to estimate a chance, so she should repeat it many times and see how often at least 8 heads come up.

solve.answer: Flip 10 times for one quiz, repeat many times, and count quizzes with at least 8 heads
solve.work: One trial = 10 flips (one quiz); repeat many trials and find the share with at least 8 heads.

questions.skill: Organize and count data from two groups
questions.stem: Group A and Group B each recorded the shoe sizes of 8 students. Group A: 6, 7, 7, 8, 6, 7, 9, 7. Group B: 7, 8, 8, 6, 9, 8, 7, 8. What fraction of all 16 students wear size 7 or smaller? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: In Group A, six sizes are 7 or smaller (6, 7, 7, 6, 7, 7). In Group B, three are (7, 6, 7). That is $6 + 3 = 9$ students out of 16, so the fraction is $\frac{9}{16}$.

questions.skill: Organize and count data from two groups
questions.stem: A school asked 120 sixth graders and 90 seventh graders whether they like a new schedule. 75 percent of the sixth graders and 60 percent of the seventh graders said yes. How many students said yes in all?
questions.solution: Sixth graders: $0.75 \times 120 = 90$ said yes. Seventh graders: $0.60 \times 90 = 54$ said yes. In all, $90 + 54 = 144$ students said yes.

questions.skill: Compare two groups with fractions, means, medians or ranges
questions.stem: A sample of 9 seventh graders has a mean of 14 minutes of daily reading. A sample of 6 sixth graders has a mean of 11 minutes of daily reading. What is the mean of all 15 students together, in minutes?
questions.solution: Total minutes for the seventh graders: $9 \times 14 = 126$. For the sixth graders: $6 \times 11 = 66$. All 15 students: $126 + 66 = 192$ minutes. The mean is $192 \div 15 = 12.8$ minutes.

questions.skill: Compare two groups with fractions, means, medians or ranges
questions.stem: Group A heights in inches: 52, 55, 49, 58, 56. Group B heights in inches: 50, 61, 47, 59, 53. How many inches greater is the range of Group B than the range of Group A?
questions.solution: Group A range: $58 - 49 = 9$. Group B range: $61 - 47 = 14$. Group B's range is $14 - 9 = 5$ inches greater.

questions.skill: Compare two groups with fractions, means, medians or ranges
questions.stem: A random sample from class A has a mean quiz score of 85, and a random sample from class B has a mean of 80. Sam says class A did better. What extra information would best help decide whether the 5-point difference is meaningful?
choices: How spread out the scores are in each sample
The first names of the students in each sample
The time of day when each class took the quiz
The color of the paper that the quiz was printed on
questions.answer: How spread out the scores are in each sample
questions.solution: If the scores in each group are spread out a lot, a 5-point difference between the means may be small by comparison. If they are tightly grouped, 5 points may be a clear difference. So knowing the variation is useful.

solve.answer: How spread out the scores are in each sample
solve.work: Whether a difference of means is meaningful depends on the variability (spread) within each sample.

questions.skill: Combine several random samples
questions.stem: Three random samples are taken from the same population. In the first, 8 of 20 people prefer tea. In the second, 14 of 30 prefer tea. In the third, 18 of 50 prefer tea. Using all three samples together, what fraction of the population would you estimate prefer tea? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Together, $8 + 14 + 18 = 40$ people prefer tea out of $20 + 30 + 50 = 100$ people. The fraction is $\frac{40}{100} = \frac{2}{5}$.

questions.skill: Combine several random samples
questions.stem: A town has 2,500 voters. Two random samples of voters were asked about a new library. In the first sample, 30 of 60 voters said yes. In the second sample, 54 of 90 voters said yes. Using both samples together, about how many of the town's voters would say yes?
questions.solution: Together, $30 + 54 = 84$ voters said yes out of $60 + 90 = 150$. That is $\frac{84}{150} = 0.56$. Then $0.56 \times 2500 = 1400$ voters.

questions.skill: Judge a conclusion drawn from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 100 people shows that 52 prefer plan A. Another random sample of 100 shows that 46 prefer plan A. Maya says that more than half of all the people prefer plan A. Which response is best?
choices: She is right, because the first sample has 52, which is more than half.
Both samples are close to half and differ, so we cannot be sure about plan A.
She is wrong, because the second sample has 46, which is less than half.
At least one of the samples must be wrong, because the two samples differ.
questions.answer: Both samples are close to half and differ, so we cannot be sure about plan A.
questions.solution: The two samples give 52% and 46%, which are both close to half and not the same. Random samples vary, so these results cannot show that more than half prefer plan A, or that fewer than half do.

solve.answer: Both samples are close to half and differ, so we cannot be sure about plan A.
solve.work: 52% and 46% straddle 50% (combined 49%); sampling variability means we cannot be sure whether more than half prefer A.

questions.skill: Judge a conclusion drawn from a sample
questions.stem: The mean amount of sleep in a random sample of 30 eighth graders is 7.5 hours a night. A student writes: "All seventh graders sleep about 7.5 hours a night." What is wrong with this conclusion?
choices: The number 7.5 is not a whole number, so it cannot be used to describe sleep.
A sample of 30 students is too large for the mean to be useful.
The sample was of eighth graders, so it says little about seventh graders.
A mean can never be used to describe the students in any group.
questions.answer: The sample was of eighth graders, so it says little about seventh graders.
questions.solution: A sample can describe the population it was taken from. These are eighth graders, so the result may not hold for seventh graders, who may sleep differently.

solve.answer: The sample was of eighth graders, so it says little about seventh graders.
solve.work: The sample is from eighth graders, a different population; it does not support a claim about seventh graders.

questions.skill: Word a survey question fairly
questions.stem: Survey 1 asks, "Do you want a pool at our school?" and 60 percent say yes. Survey 2 asks, "Nearby schools all have beautiful pools, and ours has none. Do you want a pool at our school?" and 90 percent say yes. What is the best explanation for the difference?
choices: The wording of Survey 2 leads people toward answering yes.
Survey 2 asked many more people than Survey 1 did.
Survey 1 is biased because its wording is shorter.
Percents from two different surveys can never be compared.
questions.answer: The wording of Survey 2 leads people toward answering yes.
questions.solution: Survey 2 adds sentences that make not having a pool sound bad, which nudges people to say yes. The wording, not the people's real opinion, may explain the higher percent.

solve.answer: The wording of Survey 2 leads people toward answering yes.
solve.work: Survey 2's preamble is leading wording that pushes toward yes.

questions.skill: Simulating samples
questions.stem: Students simulate choosing 20 students at random by reading random digits from 0 to 9. The digits 0, 1 and 2 stand for "walks to school", and every other digit stands for "does not walk". The 20 digits are 3, 8, 1, 0, 9, 4, 2, 7, 6, 5, 0, 2, 8, 3, 9, 1, 4, 6, 7, 2. What percent of the 20 simulated students walk to school?
questions.solution: Count the digits that are 0, 1 or 2: 1, 0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 2, which is 7 digits. So 7 of the 20 simulated students walk, and $\frac{7}{20} = \frac{35}{100}$, which is 35%.

questions.skill: Compare the centres of two data sets
questions.stem: Data set A has the values 2, 3, 3, 4, 5. Data set B has the values 6, 7, 7, 8, 9. How much greater is the median of B than the median of A?
questions.solution: The values are already in order. The middle value of A is 3. The middle value of B is 7. The difference is $7 - 3 = 4$.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two data sets
questions.stem: Data set P has the values 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. Data set Q has the values 4, 10, 14, 18, 24. Both have a median of 14. Which statement about their spread is correct?
choices: Q is more spread out, since its values go from 4 to 24
P is more spread out, since its values go from 10 to 18
They have the same spread, since the medians are equal
They have the same spread, since both have 5 values
questions.answer: Q is more spread out, since its values go from 4 to 24
questions.solution: The range of P is $18 - 10 = 8$ and the range of Q is $24 - 4 = 20$. Q's values are farther apart, so Q is more spread out. Having the same center or the same number of values does not make the spread equal.

solve.answer: Q is more spread out, since its values go from 4 to 24
solve.work: Range P = 8, range Q = 20; Q more spread out.

questions.skill: Recognize an outlier in a distribution
questions.stem: Most of the values in a data set are between 20 and 30, but one value is 75. What do we call the value 75?
choices: The median
The mode
An outlier
The mean
questions.answer: An outlier
questions.solution: A value that is far away from the rest of the data is called an outlier. The value 75 is much larger than the values between 20 and 30.

solve.answer: An outlier
solve.work: A value far from the rest is an outlier.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Ravi practiced piano for 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 minutes on five days. Lena practiced for 25, 30, 35, 40, 45 minutes on five days. How many minutes greater is Lena's mean practice time than Ravi's?
questions.solution: Ravi's mean is (15 + 20 + 25 + 30 + 35) / 5 = 125 / 5 = 25 minutes. Lena's mean is (25 + 30 + 35 + 40 + 45) / 5 = 175 / 5 = 35 minutes. The difference is 35 - 25 = 10 minutes.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: The median jump distance for a group of boys is 140 centimeters. The median jump distance for a group of girls is 152 centimeters. Which statement is correct?
choices: The girls' distances are spread out 12 centimeters more than the boys' distances.
Every girl jumped 12 centimeters farther than every boy.
The center of the girls' distances is 12 centimeters greater than the center of the boys' distances.
The center of the boys' distances is 12 centimeters greater than the center of the girls' distances.
questions.answer: The center of the girls' distances is 12 centimeters greater than the center of the boys' distances.
questions.solution: A median is a measure of center. 152 - 140 = 12, so the girls' center is 12 centimeters greater. Medians say nothing about spread, and they do not mean that every girl jumped farther than every boy.

solve.answer: The center of the girls' distances is 12 centimeters greater than the center of the boys' distances.
solve.work: Medians are measures of center: 152-140=12, girls' center greater. Spread not given; 'every girl' not supported; boys' option reversed.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: A dot plot of last week's daily high temperatures has a median of 61 degrees. This week's dot plot has exactly the same shape, but every temperature is 7 degrees higher. What is the median of this week's temperatures?
questions.solution: Moving every value up by 7 moves the center up by 7 as well, and nothing else changes. The new median is 61 + 7 = 68 degrees.

solve.work: Shifting every value by +7 shifts the median by 7: 61+7=68.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Set 1 is 3, 5, 8, 9, 10. Set 2 is 2, 6, 7, 7, 12. Which statement about the medians is correct?
choices: Set 1's median is 1 greater than Set 2's median.
Set 2's median is 2 greater than Set 1's median.
Set 2's median is 3 greater than Set 1's median.
The two medians are equal.
questions.answer: Set 1's median is 1 greater than Set 2's median.
questions.solution: Both lists are already in order. The middle value of Set 1 is 8 and the middle value of Set 2 is 7, so Set 1's median is 1 greater. (Comparing the greatest values gives 2, and comparing the ranges gives 3, but neither is a median.)

solve.answer: Set 1's median is 1 greater than Set 2's median.
solve.work: Set 1 sorted 3,5,8,9,10 median 8. Set 2 sorted 2,6,7,7,12 median 7. 8-7=1, Set 1 greater by 1.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: A dot plot of Class A's quiz scores has dots only at 7, 8 and 9. A dot plot of Class B's quiz scores has dots from 3 all the way to 10. Which statement is correct?
choices: Class A's scores are more spread out than Class B's scores.
The scores of the two classes are equally spread out.
Class B's scores are more spread out than Class A's scores.
The spread cannot be compared unless the two means are known.
questions.answer: Class B's scores are more spread out than Class A's scores.
questions.solution: Class A's dots cover only 9 - 7 = 2 units, while Class B's dots cover 10 - 3 = 7 units. The wider the dots stretch, the greater the spread, and this can be seen without knowing the means.

solve.answer: Class B's scores are more spread out than Class A's scores.
solve.work: Class A spans 7-9 (range 2); Class B spans 3-10 (range 7). B more spread out. Spread does not need means.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: On one number line, the dots of Plot A go from 12 to 20, and the dots of Plot B go from 5 to 30. How much greater is the range of Plot B than the range of Plot A?
questions.solution: The range of A is 20 - 12 = 8. The range of B is 30 - 5 = 25. The difference is 25 - 8 = 17.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Monday's temperatures, in degrees, at five times of the day were 55, 58, 61, 66, 70. Tuesday's were 52, 57, 60, 64, 65. How much greater is Monday's range than Tuesday's range?
questions.solution: Monday's range is 70 - 55 = 15 degrees. Tuesday's range is 65 - 52 = 13 degrees. The difference is 15 - 13 = 2 degrees.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Which of these describes a data set with a small spread?
choices: The values are all large numbers.
The values are all close together.
The values are listed in order from least to greatest.
The data set has only a few values.
questions.answer: The values are all close together.
questions.solution: Spread tells how far apart the values are. A small spread means the values are close together. Having large values, being in order, or having few values says nothing about spread.

solve.answer: The values are all close together.
solve.work: Small spread means values are close together.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot has 1 dot at 1, 2 dots at 2, 4 dots at 3, 2 dots at 4 and 1 dot at 5. Which describes its shape?
choices: Skewed to the right, with its peak at 1
Symmetric, with its peak at 3
Flat, with the same number of dots at each value
Symmetric, with its peak at 4
questions.answer: Symmetric, with its peak at 3
questions.solution: The counts 1, 2, 4, 2, 1 go up to the tallest stack at 3 and then come back down in the same way, so the shape is symmetric about 3, where the peak is.

solve.answer: Symmetric, with its peak at 3
solve.work: Counts 1,2,4,2,1 mirror around 3 with tallest at 3.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot has 3 dots at 2, 4 dots at 3, no dots at 4 or 5, 5 dots at 6 and 3 dots at 7. Which statement describes it?
choices: There is one cluster, with an outlier at 7.
The shape is flat, with no gaps.
There is a gap between 2 and 3.
There are two clusters, with a gap between 3 and 6.
questions.answer: There are two clusters, with a gap between 3 and 6.
questions.solution: The dots at 2 and 3 form one cluster and the dots at 6 and 7 form another. Nothing is at 4 or 5, so there is a gap between 3 and 6.

solve.answer: There are two clusters, with a gap between 3 and 6.
solve.work: Dots at 2,3 and at 6,7 with none at 4,5: two clusters separated by a gap between 3 and 6.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot of the number of brothers and sisters students have shows 4 dots at 0, 9 dots at 1, 6 dots at 2, 3 dots at 3 and 1 dot at 4. At which number is the peak, the tallest stack of dots?
questions.solution: The stacks have 4, 9, 6, 3 and 1 dots. The tallest stack, with 9 dots, is at 1, so the peak is at 1.

questions.skill: Judge the overlap of two distributions
questions.stem: On the same number line, all the dots of Plot A are from 10 to 20, and all the dots of Plot B are from 30 to 40. Which statement is correct?
choices: The plots overlap completely.
The plots overlap between 20 and 30.
The plots do not overlap: every value in Plot B is greater than every value in Plot A.
The plots overlap from 10 to 40.
questions.answer: The plots do not overlap: every value in Plot B is greater than every value in Plot A.
questions.solution: A overlaps B only if some part of the number line is covered by both. A ends at 20 and B starts at 30, so no part is covered by both. The gap between 20 and 30 has no dots from either plot.

solve.answer: The plots do not overlap: every value in Plot B is greater than every value in Plot A.
solve.work: A in [10,20], B in [30,40]; no overlap, all B values > all A values.

questions.skill: Judge the overlap of two distributions
questions.stem: On one number line, the dots of Set A go from 4 to 12 and the dots of Set B go from 9 to 20. The sets overlap where both cover the same part of the number line. How long is the overlapping part?
questions.solution: Both sets cover the part of the number line from 9 (where B starts) to 12 (where A ends). Its length is 12 - 9 = 3.

questions.skill: Plot two distributions on one number line
questions.stem: Class A's scores are 12, 15, 18 and 20. Class B's scores are 14, 16, 22 and 25. You will draw both dot plots on one number line. How many units must the number line cover, from the least score to the greatest score?
questions.solution: The least score is 12 (Class A) and the greatest is 25 (Class B). The number line must cover at least 25 - 12 = 13 units.

questions.skill: Plot two distributions on one number line
questions.stem: Set A is 3, 5, 8, 9. Set B is 6, 10, 12, 14. You want to show both sets as dot plots on one number line. Which number line can show every value?
choices: From 0 to 10, with a mark at every whole number
From 3 to 9, with a mark at every whole number
From 0 to 15, with a mark at every whole number
From 6 to 14, with a mark at every whole number
questions.answer: From 0 to 15, with a mark at every whole number
questions.solution: The values run from 3 to 14. Only a number line from 0 to 15 includes both 3 and 14. From 0 to 10 and from 3 to 9 leave out 12 and 14, and from 6 to 14 leaves out 3 and 5.

solve.answer: From 0 to 15, with a mark at every whole number
solve.work: All values from 3 to 14; only 0 to 15 contains them all.

questions.skill: Plot two distributions on one number line
questions.stem: Plot A has dots at 4, 5, 5 and 7. Plot B has dots at 5, 6, 7, 7 and 7. Both plots are drawn on one number line. How many dots are at 7 in all?
questions.solution: Plot A has 1 dot at 7 and Plot B has 3 dots at 7. In all there are 1 + 3 = 4 dots at 7.

solve.work: A has one 7, B has three 7s: 4.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: A stem-and-leaf plot shows the number of seconds students took to run a lap. The row for stem 3 has leaves 0, 2, 5. The row for stem 4 has leaves 1, 1, 7, 9. The row for stem 5 has leaves 2, 6. How many students are shown?
questions.solution: Each leaf is one student. Stem 3 has 3 leaves, stem 4 has 4 leaves and stem 5 has 2 leaves, so 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 students.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: In a stem-and-leaf plot of ages, stem 1 has leaves 1, 4, 4, 6; stem 2 has leaves 0, 3, 4, 4, 4, 9; and stem 3 has leaves 2, 5. A stem of 2 and a leaf of 4 means 24. Which age appears most often?
questions.solution: The leaf 4 appears three times on stem 2, so 24 appears 3 times. 14 appears twice and every other age appears once. The most common age is 24.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: A stem-and-leaf plot of lengths has the key 3 | 1 means 3.1 meters. One row is: 3 | 1 2 8. Which list shows the lengths in that row?
questions.solution: The stem is the ones digit and each leaf is the tenths digit. The row 3 | 1 2 8 stands for 3.1, 3.2 and 3.8 meters.

questions.skill: Read a histogram or grouped frequency table
questions.stem: A histogram shows how many books students read last year. The bars are 0 to 4 books: 5 students; 5 to 9 books: 12 students; 10 to 14 books: 8 students; 15 to 19 books: 3 students. How many students are shown?
questions.solution: Add the heights of the bars: 5 + 12 + 8 + 3 = 28 students.

questions.skill: Read a histogram or grouped frequency table
questions.stem: A histogram shows the daily high temperatures over 30 days. The bars are 50 to 59 degrees: 4 days; 60 to 69 degrees: 9 days; 70 to 79 degrees: 12 days; 80 to 89 degrees: 5 days. Which interval has the most days?
choices: 60 to 69 degrees
80 to 89 degrees
50 to 59 degrees
70 to 79 degrees
questions.answer: 70 to 79 degrees
questions.solution: The tallest bar belongs to the interval with the greatest count. The counts are 4, 9, 12 and 5, so the interval with 12 days, 70 to 79 degrees, is the tallest.

solve.answer: 70 to 79 degrees

questions.skill: Read a histogram or grouped frequency table
questions.stem: A histogram shows the ages of people at a library event. The bars are 0 to 9 years: 6 people; 10 to 19 years: 11 people; 20 to 29 years: 4 people; 30 to 39 years: 3 people. How many people are younger than 20?
questions.solution: People younger than 20 are in the first two bars: 6 + 11 = 17 people.

questions.skill: Read a box plot from its five-number summary
questions.stem: A box plot of plant heights, in centimeters, has a minimum of 8, a first quartile of 14, a median of 20, a third quartile of 30 and a maximum of 40. What is the range of the heights?
questions.solution: The range is the maximum minus the minimum: 40 - 8 = 32 centimeters.

questions.skill: Read a box plot from its five-number summary
questions.stem: A box plot of the minutes students took to get to school has a minimum of 5, a first quartile of 12, a median of 18, a third quartile of 27 and a maximum of 41. What is the interquartile range, the length of the box?
questions.solution: The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first quartile: 27 - 12 = 15 minutes.

questions.skill: Read a box plot from its five-number summary
questions.stem: About what fraction of the values in a data set lie inside the box of its box plot, between the first quartile and the third quartile?
choices: About one quarter
About three quarters
About one half
All of them
questions.answer: About one half
questions.solution: The quartiles split the data into four parts with about the same number of values. The box holds the middle two parts, which is about one half of the values.

solve.answer: About one half
solve.work: Box from Q1 to Q3 holds the middle half.

questions.skill: Draw a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: In a school race, the runners in Group A had a median time of 25 minutes. The runners in Group B had a median time of 30 minutes. The two groups had about the same spread. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Group B's times were typically greater than Group A's times.
Every runner in Group B was slower than every runner in Group A.
Group A's times were more spread out than Group B's times.
Group A's times were typically greater than Group B's times.
questions.answer: Group B's times were typically greater than Group A's times.
questions.solution: Group B's median is 5 minutes greater, so its times are typically greater. A median does not show that every runner in B was slower, and the spreads were about the same.

solve.answer: Group B's times were typically greater than Group A's times.
solve.work: Similar spread, B median 30 > A 25: B's times typically greater. 'Every runner' not supported.

questions.skill: Draw a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: A stand sold these cups of lemonade on five sunny days: 18, 20, 21, 22, 24. It sold these on five cloudy days: 14, 15, 17, 18, 19. Which statement does the data support?
choices: The stand sold more cups on every sunny day than on every cloudy day.
The sales on cloudy days had the greater range.
The stand typically sold more cups on sunny days.
The median number of cups was greater on cloudy days.
questions.answer: The stand typically sold more cups on sunny days.
questions.solution: The sunny-day median is 21 and the cloudy-day median is 17, so sunny days typically had more sales. But 18 cups were sold on a sunny day and also on a cloudy day, so it is not true for every day. The sunny days had the greater range (6 compared with 5).

solve.answer: The stand typically sold more cups on sunny days.
solve.work: Sunny median 21, range 6; cloudy median 17, range 5. Sunny typically more. Not every day: cloudy 19 > sunny 18.

questions.skill: Compare two dot plots
questions.stem: Two dot plots share one number line. Plot A has dots at 2, 3, 3, 5, 8 and 9. Plot B has dots at 4, 6, 6, 7, 9 and 9. How many more dots does Plot B have than Plot A at values greater than 5?
questions.solution: Plot B has dots at 6, 6, 7, 9 and 9 above 5, which is 5 dots. Plot A has dots at 8 and 9 above 5, which is 2 dots. The difference is $5 - 2 = 3$ dots.

questions.skill: Compare the centres of two distributions
questions.stem: Three children in Group X are 4, 6 and 8 years old. Three children in Group Y are 10, 12 and 14 years old. The ages are shown as two dot plots on one number line. How many years greater is the mean age of Group Y than the mean age of Group X?
questions.solution: The mean age of Group X is $(4 + 6 + 8) \div 3 = 6$. The mean age of Group Y is $(10 + 12 + 14) \div 3 = 12$. The difference is $12 - 6 = 6$ years. (Every age in Group Y is 6 more than the matching age in Group X.)

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Plot P has dots at 5, 5, 6, 6 and 7. Plot Q has dots at 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Both plots are drawn on one number line. Which statement is correct?
choices: Plot P's dots are more spread out than Plot Q's.
Plot P's dots are centred at a greater value than Plot Q's.
Plot Q's dots are more spread out than Plot P's.
Plot P's and Plot Q's dots are equally spread out.
questions.answer: Plot Q's dots are more spread out than Plot P's.
questions.solution: Plot P runs from 5 to 7, a range of 2. Plot Q runs from 5 to 12, a range of 7. So Plot Q is more spread out. Plot Q's dots are also centred at a greater value, so the statement about the centres is false.

solve.answer: Plot Q's dots are more spread out than Plot P's.
solve.work: P range 2, Q range 7: Q more spread out. Centres: P about 6, Q about 8, so P is not greater.

questions.skill: Compare the means of two data sets
questions.stem: Team A scored 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12 points in five games. Team B scored 7, 10, 11, 12 and 15 points in five games. How much greater is the mean of Team B's scores than the mean of Team A's scores?

questions.skill: Interpret overlapping distributions
questions.stem: Heights of plants grown with fertilizer, in centimeters, are 14, 16, 17, 18, 18 and 20. Heights of plants grown without fertilizer are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. Which statement do these data support?
choices: Every plant with fertilizer was taller than every plant without
Plants with fertilizer tended to be taller, but the two sets overlap
Plants without fertilizer tended to be taller
The two sets are centered at about the same place
questions.answer: Plants with fertilizer tended to be taller, but the two sets overlap
questions.solution: The median with fertilizer is $(17 + 18) \div 2 = 17.5$ and without is $(12 + 13) \div 2 = 12.5$, so the plants with fertilizer tended to be taller. But the sets overlap: a plant without fertilizer reached 15 centimeters, which is taller than the 14 centimeter plant that had fertilizer.

solve.answer: Plants with fertilizer tended to be taller, but the two sets overlap
solve.work: With: median 17.5; without: median 12.5, so fertilized taller. Overlap: 14 (with) is below 15 (without), so not every one taller. Overlap option is correct.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: A stem-and-leaf plot of ages has these rows: stem 1 with leaves 2, 5, 8; stem 2 with leaves 0, 3, 3, 9; stem 3 with leaves 1, 4. A stem of 2 and a leaf of 3 means 23. What is the median age?
questions.solution: The plot shows the ages 12, 15, 18, 20, 23, 23, 29, 31 and 34, which is 9 values in order. The median is the 5th value, which is 23.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Eli's six quiz scores were 72, 85, 90, 78, 80 and 87. Mia's six quiz scores were 88, 76, 94, 82, 90 and 86. How many points greater is Mia's mean score than Eli's mean score?
questions.solution: Eli's total is 492, so his mean is 492 / 6 = 82. Mia's total is 516, so her mean is 516 / 6 = 86. The difference is 86 - 82 = 4 points.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: A bus company recorded how many minutes late its buses were on six days. Route 5: 3, 6, 4, 9, 7, 5. Route 8: 8, 12, 10, 7, 14, 10. How many minutes greater is the median lateness of Route 8 than the median lateness of Route 5?
questions.solution: Put each list in order. Route 5: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, so the median is (5 + 6) / 2 = 5.5. Route 8: 7, 8, 10, 10, 12, 14, so the median is (10 + 10) / 2 = 10. The difference is 10 - 5.5 = 4.5 minutes.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Two groups of students were asked how many minutes they read each night. Group A has a mean of 18 minutes and a median of 17 minutes. Group B has a mean of 18 minutes and a median of 21 minutes. Which statement is correct?
choices: Group B's mean is 4 minutes greater than Group A's mean.
The means are equal, but Group B's median is 4 minutes greater than Group A's median.
Group A's median is 4 minutes greater than Group B's median.
The two groups have the same center by both measures.
questions.answer: The means are equal, but Group B's median is 4 minutes greater than Group A's median.
questions.solution: The means are both 18, so they are equal. The medians are 17 and 21, and 21 - 17 = 4, so Group B's median is 4 minutes greater.

solve.answer: The means are equal, but Group B's median is 4 minutes greater than Group A's median.
solve.work: Means 18 and 18 equal; medians 17 and 21, B's is 4 greater.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Team X's scores have a median of 54 and run from 40 to 70. Team Y's scores have a median of 47 and run from 30 to 80. Which statement is correct?
choices: Team Y's center is greater, because its highest score is greater.
Team Y's center is 7 points greater than Team X's center.
Team X's center is 10 points greater than Team Y's center.
Team X's center is 7 points greater than Team Y's center.
questions.answer: Team X's center is 7 points greater than Team Y's center.
questions.solution: Center is measured by the median. 54 - 47 = 7, so Team X's center is 7 points greater. The highest and lowest scores describe spread, not center.

solve.answer: Team X's center is 7 points greater than Team Y's center.
solve.work: Centers (medians) 54 and 47: X greater by 7. Highest score does not decide center.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Two groups of cyclists recorded the length of one ride, in miles. Group 1: 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 20. Group 2: 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15. How much greater is the interquartile range (IQR) of Group 1 than the IQR of Group 2?
questions.solution: Group 1: the lower half is 3, 5, 8 with median 5; the upper half is 11, 14, 20 with median 14. IQR = 14 - 5 = 9. Group 2: the lower half is 7, 8, 10 with median 8; the upper half is 12, 13, 15 with median 13. IQR = 13 - 8 = 5. The difference is 9 - 5 = 4.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Two classes took the same test. Class A's scores have a mean of 78 and a mean absolute deviation (MAD) of 3. Class B's scores have a mean of 78 and a MAD of 8. The MAD tells how far scores typically are from the mean. Which statement is correct?
choices: Class B's scores are more spread out around the same mean.
Class A's scores are more spread out, because its MAD is smaller.
The classes have the same spread, because their means are equal.
Class B's mean is higher, because its MAD is greater.
questions.answer: Class B's scores are more spread out around the same mean.
questions.solution: A greater MAD means the scores are typically farther from the mean, so Class B's scores are more spread out. The means are equal, and the MAD does not change the mean.

solve.answer: Class B's scores are more spread out around the same mean.
solve.work: Same mean; larger MAD means more spread. B's MAD 8 > A's 3, so B more spread around same mean.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Plot A has dots at 12, 12, 13, 15, 18. Plot B has dots at 10, 14, 14, 15, 16, 22. The range of Plot B is how many times the range of Plot A?
questions.solution: The range of A is 18 - 12 = 6. The range of B is 22 - 10 = 12. Since 12 / 6 = 2, the range of B is 2 times the range of A.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Set M has a range of 30 and an interquartile range of 8. Set N has a range of 22 and an interquartile range of 12. Which statement is correct?
choices: Set M is more spread out by both measures, because its range is greater.
Set N is more spread out by both measures, because its IQR is greater.
The two sets are equally spread out, because their ranges and IQRs are close.
The middle half of the values is more spread out in Set N, though Set M has the greater range.
questions.answer: The middle half of the values is more spread out in Set N, though Set M has the greater range.
questions.solution: Set M has the greater range (30 > 22), but Set N has the greater IQR (12 > 8). So the whole data set is more stretched out in M, while the middle half of the values is more spread out in N. Neither set is greater by both measures.

solve.answer: The middle half of the values is more spread out in Set N, though Set M has the greater range.
solve.work: IQR (middle half spread): N 12 > M 8. Range: M 30 > N 22. So measures disagree.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot shows how many books 14 students read last month: 5 dots at 1, 4 dots at 2, 3 dots at 3, 1 dot at 7 and 1 dot at 9. Which describes the shape?
choices: Most values are low, with a tail stretching toward the high values.
Most values are high, with a tail stretching toward the low values.
The values are balanced evenly on both sides of the center.
The values form two clusters of equal size.
questions.answer: Most values are low, with a tail stretching toward the high values.
questions.solution: The tallest stacks are at the low values 1, 2 and 3, and a few dots trail off toward 7 and 9. A tail toward the high values is called skewed to the right.

solve.answer: Most values are low, with a tail stretching toward the high values.
solve.work: Most dots at 1-3, a few far out at 7 and 9: right tail toward high values.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot of 18 values has 2 dots at 10, 3 dots at 11, 4 dots at 12, 3 dots at 13, 5 dots at 20 and 1 dot at 21. There is a gap between 13 and 20 that splits the dots into two clusters. How many dots are in the lower cluster?
questions.solution: The lower cluster is the dots from 10 to 13: 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 12 dots. (The upper cluster has 5 + 1 = 6 dots, and 12 + 6 = 18.)

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot has the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 on its number line. Each choice gives the number of dots at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, in that order. Which choice gives a symmetric shape?
questions.solution: A symmetric shape matches on the two sides of its center. 1, 3, 5, 3, 1 reads the same forward and backward. 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 slope one way, and 2, 5, 1, 4, 3 has no matching sides.

solve.work: 1,3,5,3,1 reads the same both ways about 3.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot has 3 dots at each of the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Which describes its shape?
choices: Skewed to the left, with a tail toward 1.
Flat: every value has the same number of dots, and there is no single peak.
One cluster with an outlier at 6.
A peak in the middle, with fewer dots at each end.
questions.answer: Flat: every value has the same number of dots, and there is no single peak.
questions.solution: Every value from 1 to 6 has exactly 3 dots, so no stack is taller than another. The shape is flat (uniform), with no peak, no gap and no outlier.

solve.answer: Flat: every value has the same number of dots, and there is no single peak.
solve.work: Equal counts everywhere: flat/uniform, no peak.

questions.skill: Judge the overlap of two distributions
questions.stem: Set A is 22, 24, 25, 27, 28. Set B is 26, 28, 29, 30, 32. Which statement is correct?
choices: The sets do not overlap at all.
The sets overlap a little, and Set B's values are generally greater.
The sets overlap a little, and Set A's values are generally greater.
The sets overlap almost completely, and Set A's values are generally greater.
questions.answer: The sets overlap a little, and Set B's values are generally greater.
questions.solution: Set A goes up to 28 and Set B starts at 26, so the sets share the values from 26 to 28: a small overlap. Set B's median, 29, is greater than Set A's median, 25, so B's values are generally greater.

solve.answer: The sets overlap a little, and Set B's values are generally greater.
solve.work: A 22-28 (median 25), B 26-32 (median 29). Overlap only 26-28; B generally greater.

questions.skill: Judge the overlap of two distributions
questions.stem: Without extra water, six sunflowers had heights, in centimeters, of 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18. With extra water, six sunflowers had heights of 15, 17, 19, 20, 22, 24. How many of the heights with extra water are inside the interval from the least to the greatest height without extra water?
questions.solution: Without extra water the heights run from 11 to 18. Of the heights with extra water, only 15 and 17 are between 11 and 18 (19 and above are too tall). So 2 of them are inside.

solve.work: Without water: 11 to 18. With water values in [11,18]: 15, 17. Count 2.

questions.skill: Judge the overlap of two distributions
questions.stem: Set A's values run from 30 to 70 with a median of 50. Set B's values run from 34 to 74 with a median of 54. Which statement is correct?
choices: The sets overlap a lot, so the 4-point difference in medians is small compared with the spread.
Set B is clearly higher, because its median is greater.
The sets do not overlap, because their medians are different.
The sets overlap only a little, because the medians are not equal.
questions.answer: The sets overlap a lot, so the 4-point difference in medians is small compared with the spread.
questions.solution: Both sets stretch across about 40 units, and they share all the values from 34 to 70. A 4-point difference between medians is small next to that spread, so the sets overlap a lot even though the medians are different.

solve.answer: The sets overlap a lot, so the 4-point difference in medians is small compared with the spread.
solve.work: Ranges 30-70 and 34-74 overlap 34-70 (most of both). Median gap 4 vs range 40: small difference.

questions.skill: Plot two distributions on one number line
questions.stem: Why should two dot plots that are being compared be drawn on the same number line, with the same scale?
choices: So both plots will have the same number of dots.
So both plots will have the same mean.
So both plots will have the same range.
So the positions of the dots can be compared directly.
questions.answer: So the positions of the dots can be compared directly.
questions.solution: Only when both plots use the same scale does a dot that is farther right mean a greater value in either plot. The number of dots, the mean and the range depend on the data, not on how the line is drawn.

solve.answer: So the positions of the dots can be compared directly.
solve.work: Same scale lets dot positions be compared directly; it does not change means, ranges or counts.

questions.skill: Plot two distributions on one number line
questions.stem: Group A's heights run from 140 to 185 centimeters. Group B's heights run from 152 to 190 centimeters. Which is the best number line for drawing both dot plots?
choices: From 0 to 200, with a mark every 50 centimeters
From 150 to 200, with a mark every 10 centimeters
From 140 to 190, with a mark every 5 centimeters
From 140 to 185, with a mark every 5 centimeters
questions.answer: From 140 to 190, with a mark every 5 centimeters
questions.solution: The line must reach from the least value, 140, to the greatest value, 190, and marks every 5 centimeters make it easy to place the dots. From 0 to 200 with marks every 50 is too coarse, and the other two lines cut off the heights from 140 to 149 or the heights above 185.

solve.answer: From 140 to 190, with a mark every 5 centimeters
solve.work: Need 140 to 190. 150-200 misses 140-149; 140-185 misses 186-190; 0-200 by 50s too coarse. Best: 140-190 by 5s.

questions.skill: Plot two distributions on one number line
questions.stem: Plot A has dots at 2, 4, 4, 6. Plot B has dots at 3, 4, 5, 5, 9. The two plots are drawn together on one number line, so there are 9 dots in all. What is the median of the 9 values?
questions.solution: Put all 9 values in order: 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 9. The middle (5th) value is 4.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: A stem-and-leaf plot shows the weights of ten dogs in pounds. Stem 5 has leaves 2, 4, 7. Stem 6 has leaves 0, 1, 5, 5, 8. Stem 7 has leaves 3, 6. A stem of 5 and a leaf of 2 means 52. What is the median weight?
questions.solution: The ten weights in order are 52, 54, 57, 60, 61, 65, 65, 68, 73, 76. With 10 values, the median is the mean of the 5th and 6th: (61 + 65) / 2 = 63.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: Two classes took a quiz. Class A: stem 6 has leaves 5, 8; stem 7 has leaves 0, 2, 4, 6; stem 8 has leaves 1, 5. Class B: stem 6 has leaves 0, 2; stem 7 has leaves 3, 5, 5; stem 8 has leaves 0, 2, 7, 9. A stem of 8 and a leaf of 1 means 81. How many more students in Class B than in Class A scored 80 or above?
questions.solution: Class A has two scores of 80 or above (81 and 85). Class B has four (80, 82, 87 and 89). The difference is 4 - 2 = 2 students.

questions.skill: Read a stem-and-leaf plot
questions.stem: A stem-and-leaf plot has these rows: stem 2 with leaves 1, 3, 3, 8; stem 3 with leaves 0, 4, 5; stem 4 with leaf 2. A stem of 2 and a leaf of 1 means 21. Which statement is true?
choices: Exactly half of the values are in the 20s.
The median is 30.
The range is 31.
The mode is 3.
questions.answer: Exactly half of the values are in the 20s.
questions.solution: The values are 21, 23, 23, 28, 30, 34, 35, 42. Four of the eight are in the 20s, which is half. The median is (28 + 30) / 2 = 29, the range is 42 - 21 = 21, and the mode is 23 (the leaf 3 appears twice, but the value is 23).

solve.answer: Exactly half of the values are in the 20s.
solve.work: Values 21,23,23,28,30,34,35,42 (8). In 20s: 4 of 8 = half (true). Mode 23 not 3; range 21 not 31; median (28+30)/2=29 not 30.

questions.skill: Read a histogram or grouped frequency table
questions.stem: A histogram shows the minutes 25 students spent on homework. The bars are 0 to 9 minutes: 3 students; 10 to 19 minutes: 7 students; 20 to 29 minutes: 9 students; 30 to 39 minutes: 4 students; 40 to 49 minutes: 2 students. How many students spent at least 20 minutes but fewer than 40 minutes?
questions.solution: The intervals from 20 up to (not including) 40 are 20 to 29 and 30 to 39. They hold 9 + 4 = 13 students.

questions.skill: Read a histogram or grouped frequency table
questions.stem: A histogram of 40 quiz scores has these bars: 0 to 9: 7 scores; 10 to 19: 12 scores; 20 to 29: 10 scores; 30 to 39: 11 scores. In which interval is the median score?
choices: 0 to 9
questions.solution: With 40 scores the median is between the 20th and 21st scores. Counting up from the left: 7 scores are in the first bar and 7 + 12 = 19 by the end of the second. The 20th and 21st scores are in the third bar, 20 to 29. (The tallest bar, 10 to 19, does not hold the middle.)

solve.work: 40 scores, median between 20th and 21st. Cumulative 7, 19, 29, 40: both in 20-29.

questions.skill: Read a histogram or grouped frequency table
questions.stem: A histogram shows the heights of 20 bean plants. The bars are 10 to 19 centimeters: 3 plants; 20 to 29 centimeters: 8 plants; 30 to 39 centimeters: 6 plants; 40 to 49 centimeters: 3 plants. What fraction of the plants are at least 30 centimeters tall?
questions.solution: The plants that are at least 30 centimeters tall are in the last two bars: 6 + 3 = 9 plants. That is 9 out of 20, or 9/20.

questions.skill: Read a box plot from its five-number summary
questions.stem: Box plot A has a first quartile of 20 and a third quartile of 30. Box plot B has a first quartile of 25 and a third quartile of 55. The box of plot B is how many times as long as the box of plot A?
questions.solution: The box of A has length 30 - 20 = 10. The box of B has length 55 - 25 = 30. Since 30 / 10 = 3, the box of B is 3 times as long.

questions.skill: Read a box plot from its five-number summary
questions.stem: Each box plot is summarized by its minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum. Plot P: 12, 20, 25, 30, 40. Plot Q: 22, 26, 30, 34, 38. Which statement is correct?
choices: Plot P's median is greater, and Plot P is more spread out by both its range and its IQR.
Plot Q's median is greater, and Plot Q is more spread out by both its range and its IQR.
Plot Q's median is greater, but Plot Q has the greater range.
Plot Q's median is greater, but Plot P is more spread out by both its range and its IQR.
questions.answer: Plot Q's median is greater, but Plot P is more spread out by both its range and its IQR.
questions.solution: The medians are 25 and 30, so Q's is greater. Plot P has a range of 40 - 12 = 28 and an IQR of 30 - 20 = 10. Plot Q has a range of 38 - 22 = 16 and an IQR of 34 - 26 = 8. P is more spread out by both measures.

solve.answer: Plot Q's median is greater, but Plot P is more spread out by both its range and its IQR.
solve.work: P: median 25, range 28, IQR 10. Q: median 30, range 16, IQR 8. Q's median greater; P more spread by both.

questions.skill: Read a box plot from its five-number summary
questions.stem: A box plot shows the finishing times of 60 runners. The third quartile is 14 minutes. About how many runners had a time greater than 14 minutes?
questions.solution: One quarter of the values lie above the third quartile. One quarter of 60 is 60 / 4 = 15 runners.

solve.work: About a quarter of values exceed Q3: 60/4=15.

questions.skill: Draw a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: Commute times in minutes for five people in Town A were 10, 12, 15, 18, 20. For five people in Town B they were 8, 14, 16, 22, 40. Which statement is NOT supported by the data?
choices: Town B has the greater range of commute times.
Town A's commute times are more spread out than Town B's.
Town B's median commute time is greater than Town A's.
Town B's longest commute is longer than Town A's longest commute.
questions.answer: Town A's commute times are more spread out than Town B's.
questions.solution: Town A's range is 20 - 10 = 10 minutes and Town B's range is 40 - 8 = 32 minutes, so Town B is the more spread out. The other three statements are true: B's range is greater, B's median (16) is greater than A's (15), and 40 is greater than 20.

solve.answer: Town A's commute times are more spread out than Town B's.
solve.work: A: range 10, median 15. B: range 32, median 16, max 40. A more spread out is false.

questions.skill: Draw a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: Tara scored 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 points in five games. Uri scored 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 points in five games. Both have a mean of 10 points. Which statement is best supported by the data?
choices: Uri was more consistent, because his scores vary more.
Neither was more consistent, because their means are equal.
Tara was more consistent, because her scores vary less.
Uri was more consistent, because he had the greatest score.
questions.answer: Tara was more consistent, because her scores vary less.
questions.solution: Tara's scores stay within 4 points of each other and Uri's differ by 16, so Tara's scores vary less: she was more consistent. Equal means do not make equal consistency, and one high score does not make a player consistent.

solve.answer: Tara was more consistent, because her scores vary less.
solve.work: Tara range 4, Uri range 16: Tara varies less, more consistent.

questions.skill: Draw a conclusion the data support
questions.stem: Group A walked between 4 and 12 thousand steps a day, with a median of 8. Group B walked between 5 and 13 thousand steps a day, with a median of 9. A student says, "Every person in Group B walks more than every person in Group A." Which reply is best?
choices: No: Group A's greatest value, 12, is greater than Group B's least value, 5.
Yes: Group B has the greater median, 9, so all of its values are greater.
Yes: Group B's greatest value, 13, is greater than Group A's greatest value, 12.
No: both groups have a range of 8, so the two groups must be identical.
questions.answer: No: Group A's greatest value, 12, is greater than Group B's least value, 5.
questions.solution: The claim is about every person, so one counterexample is enough. Group A has a value of 12, which is more than Group B's least value of 5. So some person in Group A walks more than some person in Group B, and the claim is not supported. A greater median or a greater maximum does not mean every value is greater, and equal ranges do not make two groups identical.

solve.answer: No: Group A's greatest value, 12, is greater than Group B's least value, 5.
solve.work: Ranges overlap (A up to 12, B from 5), so someone in A may walk more than someone in B. The correct reply cites that overlap.

questions.skill: Compare mean and median of two sets
questions.stem: Data set P has the values 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. Data set Q has the values 18, 19, 20, 21, 42. Which statement is true?
choices: The means are equal, but Q has the greater median
The medians are equal, but Q has the greater mean
The medians and the means are both equal
Q has both the greater median and the greater mean
questions.answer: The medians are equal, but Q has the greater mean
questions.solution: Both sets have a middle value of 20, so the medians are equal. The mean of P is $100 \div 5 = 20$. The mean of Q is $120 \div 5 = 24$. The large value 42 pulls the mean of Q up but does not change its median.

solve.answer: The medians are equal, but Q has the greater mean
solve.work: Both medians 20. Mean P = 100/5 = 20; mean Q = 120/5 = 24.

questions.skill: Compare medians of sets with an even count
questions.stem: Set A has the values 14, 9, 21, 12, 17, 15. Set B has the values 22, 30, 25, 28, 27, 24. How much greater is the median of Set B than the median of Set A?
questions.solution: Order Set A: 9, 12, 14, 15, 17, 21. With 6 values, the median is the mean of the middle two: $(14 + 15) \div 2 = 14.5$. Order Set B: 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30. Its median is $(25 + 27) \div 2 = 26$. The difference is $26 - 14.5 = 11.5$.

solve.work: A sorted: 9, 12, 14, 15, 17, 21; median 14.5. B sorted: 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30; median 26. Difference 11.5.

questions.skill: Read two distributions plotted together
questions.stem: Two dot plots share one number line, and both have a mean of 5. Plot X has 1 dot at 3, 2 dots at 4, 6 dots at 5, 2 dots at 6 and 1 dot at 7. Plot Y has 4 dots at 2, 4 dots at 5 and 4 dots at 8. In all, how many dots (from both plots) are 2 or more units away from 5?
questions.solution: Dots 2 or more units from 5 are at values 3 or less, or 7 or more. In plot X, that is 1 dot at 3 and 1 dot at 7, which is 2 dots. In plot Y, the 4 dots at 2 and the 4 dots at 8 qualify, which is 8 dots. In all, $2 + 8 = 10$ dots.

solve.work: X: dots at 3 and 7 are 2 away: 1 + 1 = 2. Y: dots at 2 and 8 are 3 away: 4 + 4 = 8. Total 10. (Means check: X 60/12 = 5, Y 60/12 = 5.)

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Set P is 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Set Q has five values. Four of them are 10, 12, 15 and 17. The mean of Set Q is 4 greater than the mean of Set P. What is the fifth value of Set Q?
questions.solution: The mean of Set P is 60 / 5 = 12, so the mean of Set Q is 16. Five values with a mean of 16 add to 16 x 5 = 80. The four known values add to 54, so the fifth value is 80 - 54 = 26.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Jo's steps on 8 days, in hundreds of steps, were 31, 28, 35, 30, 34, 29, 36, 37. Kai's steps on 7 days, in hundreds of steps, were 40, 38, 45, 42, 37, 44, 41. By how many hundreds of steps is the median of Kai's days greater than the median of Jo's days?
questions.solution: Jo in order: 28, 29, 30, 31, 34, 35, 36, 37. With 8 values the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th: (31 + 34) / 2 = 32.5. Kai in order: 37, 38, 40, 41, 42, 44, 45. The middle (4th) value is 41. The difference is 41 - 32.5 = 8.5.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Each choice shows two small data sets, A and B. In which choice is the median of B exactly 3 greater than the median of A?
questions.solution: For A: 2, 5, 9 and B: 3, 8, 9 the medians are 5 and 8, which differ by 3. For A: 2, 5, 11 and B: 3, 6, 18 the means differ by 3 (6 and 9), but the medians are 5 and 6. For A: 1, 6, 8 and B: 2, 4, 11 the greatest values differ by 3, but the medians are 6 and 4. For A: 6, 2, 9 and B: 4, 5, 8 the lists are not in order; the true medians are 6 and 5.

solve.work: A: medians 5 and 8, diff 3. B: 6 and 4. C: A sorted 2,6,9 median 6; B 4,5,8 median 5. D: 5 and 6. Only first choice works.

questions.skill: Compare the centers of two distributions
questions.stem: Set A has 8 values that add to 168. Set B also has 8 values, and the mean of Set B is 6 greater than the mean of Set A. What is the sum of the values in Set B?
questions.solution: The mean of Set A is 168 / 8 = 21. The mean of Set B is 21 + 6 = 27. Eight values with a mean of 27 add to 27 x 8 = 216. (Check: the sum rises by 6 for each of the 8 values, 48, and 168 + 48 = 216.)

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Set A is 12, 15, 19, 22, 27, 30. Set B has the same least value as Set A, and its range is 7 greater than the range of Set A. What is the greatest value in Set B?
questions.solution: The range of A is 30 - 12 = 18. The range of B is 18 + 7 = 25. B starts at 12, so its greatest value is 12 + 25 = 37.

solve.work: Range A 30-12=18. Range B 25. Least 12, greatest 12+25=37.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Eight students in Group A solved a puzzle in 22, 14, 30, 18, 26, 16, 34, 20 minutes. Eight students in Group B solved it in 19, 25, 21, 23, 27, 20, 24, 22 minutes. How much greater is the interquartile range of Group A's times than that of Group B's times?

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Every value in a data set is increased by 5. How do the mean and the range of the data change?
choices: The mean increases by 5, and the range increases by 5.
The mean stays the same, and the range increases by 5.
The mean increases by 5, and the range stays the same.
The mean and the range both stay the same.
questions.answer: The mean increases by 5, and the range stays the same.
questions.solution: Adding 5 to every value slides the whole data set 5 units to the right, so the mean (and median) go up by 5. The distances between the values do not change, so the range is the same. Try 2, 4, 6: the range is 4 and the mean is 4; after adding 5 they are 7, 9, 11 with range 4 and mean 9.

solve.answer: The mean increases by 5, and the range stays the same.
solve.work: Adding 5 shifts mean by 5; max-min unchanged so range same.

questions.skill: Compare the spread of two distributions
questions.stem: Plot A has 2 dots at 10 and 2 dots at 30. Plot B has 4 dots at 20. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both plots have a mean of 20, but Plot A is more spread out.
Plot B has the greater mean, because its dots are stacked.
The plots have the same spread, because they have the same mean.
Both plots have a mean of 20, but Plot B is more spread out.
questions.answer: Both plots have a mean of 20, but Plot A is more spread out.
questions.solution: Plot A: (10 + 10 + 30 + 30) / 4 = 20. Plot B: (20 + 20 + 20 + 20) / 4 = 20. The means are equal. Plot A has a range of 20 and Plot B has a range of 0, so A is more spread out. Equal means do not mean equal spread.

solve.answer: Both plots have a mean of 20, but Plot A is more spread out.
solve.work: A mean (10+10+30+30)/4=20, B mean 20. A spread 20, B spread 0. A more spread out.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot has dots at 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 12, so most dots are at low values and one dot is far to the right. Which statement is true?
choices: The mean is less than the median, because of the dot at 12.
The mean and the median are equal, because the plot is balanced.
The median is greater than 5, because of the dot at 12.
The mean is greater than the median, because of the dot at 12.
questions.answer: The mean is greater than the median, because of the dot at 12.
questions.solution: The sum is 33, so the mean is 33 / 9, about 3.7. The middle (5th) value is 3, so the median is 3. A long tail of high values pulls the mean up toward the tail, but it barely moves the median.

solve.answer: The mean is greater than the median, because of the dot at 12.
solve.work: Sum 1+1+2+2+3+3+4+5+12=33, mean 33/9 ~ 3.67. Median 5th of 9 = 3. Mean > median, pulled up by 12.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A symmetric dot plot has 1 dot at 2, 2 dots at 3, 3 dots at 4, 6 dots at 5, 3 dots at 6, 2 dots at 7 and 1 dot at 8. How many dots are within 1 unit of the peak, counting the dots at the peak itself?
questions.solution: The peak is at 5, the tallest stack. Within 1 unit of 5 are the values 4, 5 and 6, which have 3 + 6 + 3 = 12 dots.

solve.work: Peak at 5 (6 dots). Within 1 unit: values 4,5,6 -> 3+6+3=12.

questions.skill: Describe the shape of a distribution
questions.stem: A dot plot has dots at 14, 15, 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, 17, 18, 31. The dot at 31 is far from all the others. What happens when that one dot is removed?
